deduped_items.title: Why is Xiaomi doubling down on in-house chips despite profit slump?
deduped_items.summary: Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs. On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone. The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI.
deduped_items.body_text:
Why is Xiaomi doubling down on in-house chips despite profit slump?
Chinese tech giant’s Xring O3 3nm AI processor scheduled to debut aboard folding smartphone in September
Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs.
On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone.
The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI accelerator designed to boost Xiaomi’s MiMo large language model when paired with the O3 – alongside a 3nm Xring D100 chip for autonomous driving. Xiaomi said both the O100 and D100 will be deployed commercially next year.
Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said Xiaomi’s semiconductor progress placed it in “the top tier of China’s self-developed mobile systems-on-a-chip (SoC)”.
“In the current age of AI, on-chip AI performance has become even more critical as AI workloads are becoming more complex,” Lam said, adding that while semiconductor investments yielded no immediate financial returns, Xiaomi’s long-term commitment remained positive.
Xiaomi’s chip expansion comes as the global smartphone industry grapples with surging memory and component costs, squeezing profit margins across handsets and electric vehicles.

Chinese tech giant’s Xring O3 3nm AI processor scheduled to debut aboard folding smartphone in September
Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs.
On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone.
The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI accelerator designed to boost Xiaomi’s MiMo large language model when paired with the O3 – alongside a 3nm Xring D100 chip for autonomous driving. Xiaomi said both the O100 and D100 will be deployed commercially next year.
Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said Xiaomi’s semiconductor progress placed it in “the top tier of China’s self-developed mobile systems-on-a-chip (SoC)”.
“In the current age of AI, on-chip AI performance has become even more critical as AI workloads are becoming more complex,” Lam said, adding that while semiconductor investments yielded no immediate financial returns, Xiaomi’s long-term commitment remained positive.
Xiaomi’s chip expansion comes as the global smartphone industry grapples with surging memory and component costs, squeezing profit margins across handsets and electric vehicles.

deduped_items.summary: Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs. On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone. The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI.
deduped_items.body_text:
Why is Xiaomi doubling down on in-house chips despite profit slump?
Chinese tech giant’s Xring O3 3nm AI processor scheduled to debut aboard folding smartphone in September
Xiaomi’s long-term push into proprietary silicon is laying the groundwork for complex artificial intelligence workloads on smartphones and cars, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant doubles down on self-developed chips despite an earnings slump and soaring component costs.
On Monday it unveiled its flagship Xring O3 3-nanometre AI processor for smartphones, which is scheduled to debut in September aboard its Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone.
The company has also introduced the Xring O100 – a 6nm AI accelerator designed to boost Xiaomi’s MiMo large language model when paired with the O3 – alongside a 3nm Xring D100 chip for autonomous driving. Xiaomi said both the O100 and D100 will be deployed commercially next year.
Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said Xiaomi’s semiconductor progress placed it in “the top tier of China’s self-developed mobile systems-on-a-chip (SoC)”.
“In the current age of AI, on-chip AI performance has become even more critical as AI workloads are becoming more complex,” Lam said, adding that while semiconductor investments yielded no immediate financial returns, Xiaomi’s long-term commitment remained positive.
Xiaomi’s chip expansion comes as the global smartphone industry grapples with surging memory and component costs, squeezing profit margins across handsets and electric vehicles.

deduped_items.body_text:
達卡拉力賽王者回歸！三菱宣布 Pajero 9 月 2 日全球首演
Mitsubishi Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演。
三菱（Mitsubishi）在 5 月底時宣布創下 7 連霸紀錄，贏得 12 次總冠軍的 Mitsubishi Pajero 將重出江湖，今（25）日在 Pajero 專屬網頁上宣布，Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演，重新將這款經典越野休旅帶回來。
在 Pajero 專屬網頁裡，Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點，並且刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
動力則可能採現行 Triton 的 2.4 升渦輪柴油引擎配置，具備 204 匹最大馬力、47.9 公斤米峰值扭力的輸出，滿足越野環境的使用需求。
Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點。
字母裡，還刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
Mitsubishi 先前也透過 Star Camp 2026 品牌活動，舉辦大改款 Pajero 搶先賞車會，邀請現行 Pajero 車主及品牌支持者提前一睹大改款 Pajero 風采，而不少看過的人都給出相當高的評價，表示「外型比預期的還酷」、「內裝質感很好，空間也非常大」及「迫不及待想把車開回家」，讓人對於大改款 Pajero 有著更多期待。
Pajero 於 1982 年推出，是品牌標誌性越野 SUV，從 1983 年起參加達卡拉力賽，取得輝煌成績，後來更衍伸出 Pajero mini、Pajero iO 等版本，歷經四代車型，在全球 170 多個國家和地區售出超過 325 萬輛，如今這個品牌越野神主牌再次復活，也象徵著 Mitsubishi 即將重拾當年 Pajero 在達卡拉力賽的輝煌。

達卡拉力賽王者回歸！三菱宣布 Pajero 9 月 2 日全球首演
Mitsubishi Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演。
三菱（Mitsubishi）在 5 月底時宣布創下 7 連霸紀錄，贏得 12 次總冠軍的 Mitsubishi Pajero 將重出江湖，今（25）日在 Pajero 專屬網頁上宣布，Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演，重新將這款經典越野休旅帶回來。
在 Pajero 專屬網頁裡，Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點，並且刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
動力則可能採現行 Triton 的 2.4 升渦輪柴油引擎配置，具備 204 匹最大馬力、47.9 公斤米峰值扭力的輸出，滿足越野環境的使用需求。
Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點。
字母裡，還刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
Mitsubishi 先前也透過 Star Camp 2026 品牌活動，舉辦大改款 Pajero 搶先賞車會，邀請現行 Pajero 車主及品牌支持者提前一睹大改款 Pajero 風采，而不少看過的人都給出相當高的評價，表示「外型比預期的還酷」、「內裝質感很好，空間也非常大」及「迫不及待想把車開回家」，讓人對於大改款 Pajero 有著更多期待。
Pajero 於 1982 年推出，是品牌標誌性越野 SUV，從 1983 年起參加達卡拉力賽，取得輝煌成績，後來更衍伸出 Pajero mini、Pajero iO 等版本，歷經四代車型，在全球 170 多個國家和地區售出超過 325 萬輛，如今這個品牌越野神主牌再次復活，也象徵著 Mitsubishi 即將重拾當年 Pajero 在達卡拉力賽的輝煌。

達卡拉力賽王者回歸！三菱宣布 Pajero 9 月 2 日全球首演
Mitsubishi Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演。
三菱（Mitsubishi）在 5 月底時宣布創下 7 連霸紀錄，贏得 12 次總冠軍的 Mitsubishi Pajero 將重出江湖，今（25）日在 Pajero 專屬網頁上宣布，Pajero 將於 9 月 2 日進行全球首演，重新將這款經典越野休旅帶回來。
在 Pajero 專屬網頁裡，Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點，並且刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
動力則可能採現行 Triton 的 2.4 升渦輪柴油引擎配置，具備 204 匹最大馬力、47.9 公斤米峰值扭力的輸出，滿足越野環境的使用需求。
Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點。
字母裡，還刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
Mitsubishi 先前也透過 Star Camp 2026 品牌活動，舉辦大改款 Pajero 搶先賞車會，邀請現行 Pajero 車主及品牌支持者提前一睹大改款 Pajero 風采，而不少看過的人都給出相當高的評價，表示「外型比預期的還酷」、「內裝質感很好，空間也非常大」及「迫不及待想把車開回家」，讓人對於大改款 Pajero 有著更多期待。
Pajero 於 1982 年推出，是品牌標誌性越野 SUV，從 1983 年起參加達卡拉力賽，取得輝煌成績，後來更衍伸出 Pajero mini、Pajero iO 等版本，歷經四代車型，在全球 170 多個國家和地區售出超過 325 萬輛，如今這個品牌越野神主牌再次復活，也象徵著 Mitsubishi 即將重拾當年 Pajero 在達卡拉力賽的輝煌。

動力則可能採現行 Triton 的 2.4 升渦輪柴油引擎配置，具備 204 匹最大馬力、47.9 公斤米峰值扭力的輸出，滿足越野環境的使用需求。
Mitsubishi 製作一組動畫，透過 Pajero 這六個字母，在裡頭透露這次 Pajero 的各種特點。
字母裡，還刻意以沙土方式呈現，訴說著 Pajero 一貫的越野本質。
Mitsubishi 先前也透過 Star Camp 2026 品牌活動，舉辦大改款 Pajero 搶先賞車會，邀請現行 Pajero 車主及品牌支持者提前一睹大改款 Pajero 風采，而不少看過的人都給出相當高的評價，表示「外型比預期的還酷」、「內裝質感很好，空間也非常大」及「迫不及待想把車開回家」，讓人對於大改款 Pajero 有著更多期待。
Pajero 於 1982 年推出，是品牌標誌性越野 SUV，從 1983 年起參加達卡拉力賽，取得輝煌成績，後來更衍伸出 Pajero mini、Pajero iO 等版本，歷經四代車型，在全球 170 多個國家和地區售出超過 325 萬輛，如今這個品牌越野神主牌再次復活，也象徵著 Mitsubishi 即將重拾當年 Pajero 在達卡拉力賽的輝煌。

deduped_items.title: North Korea cracks down on ghostwritten graduation theses at Pyongyang universities
deduped_items.summary: North Korea’s Cabinet Ministry of Education has ordered major universities in Pyongyang to stamp out the ghostwriting of graduation theses, sparking anxiety among soon-to-graduate students and their faculty advisers, according to a source inside the country. The education ministry issued the directive in mid-August, telling each central university to “thoroughly eliminate” the practice of writing […]
deduped_items.body_text:
North Korea’s Cabinet Ministry of Education has ordered major universities in Pyongyang to stamp out the ghostwriting of graduation theses, sparking anxiety among soon-to-graduate students and their faculty advisers, according to a source inside the country.
The education ministry issued the directive in mid-August, telling each central university to “thoroughly eliminate” the practice of writing theses on students’ behalf, a Daily NK source in Pyongyang said Monday. Intensive inspections into how graduating students prepare their theses are expected to run for about a month.
Inspectors are expected to focus on whether students personally chose their thesis topics and took part themselves in gathering research materials and drafting their papers, the source said. For students who have already finished their theses, examiners plan to check whether they understand the material well enough to explain it in their own words.
It remains unclear whether the ministry will lead the inspections directly, hand the task to the Pyongyang city department of education, or have universities cross-check each other’s students, according to the source.
Theses often treated as mere formality
Ghostwriting graduation theses is reportedly common at North Korean universities. Unlike science and engineering-focused schools such as Kim Chaek University of Technology or Pyongyang Medical University, some humanities departments treat a passing thesis as good enough, even without meaningful research, the source said.
“At some liberal arts universities, there’s a strong belief that all that matters is getting the thesis approved, even without any notable research achievement,” the source said. “The thesis is treated as just a formality to earn a diploma, and it’s rare to hear of anyone failing to graduate because of their thesis.”
As a result, some students have prepared for graduation by asking classmates or underclassmen skilled at writing to complete their entire thesis for them, the source said.
With news of the crackdown spreading, universities are anxious about being caught up in the fallout. Ahead of the formal inspections, schools have reportedly begun reviewing graduating students’ thesis preparation on their own. Some are requiring students to document how they gathered materials and drafted their papers, while in certain departments, faculty advisers are holding one-on-one interviews with students to directly confirm their thesis topics and content.
“Students who already received help from someone else, or whose thesis preparation is lacking, are on edge, worried that problems could surface during the university’s internal review,” the source said. “Ghostwriting is not only a problem for students, since the faculty members who supervised the thesis cannot escape responsibility either, so professors are just as on edge.”

deduped_items.body_text:
North Korea’s Cabinet Ministry of Education has ordered major universities in Pyongyang to stamp out the ghostwriting of graduation theses, sparking anxiety among soon-to-graduate students and their faculty advisers, according to a source inside the country.
The education ministry issued the directive in mid-August, telling each central university to “thoroughly eliminate” the practice of writing theses on students’ behalf, a Daily NK source in Pyongyang said Monday. Intensive inspections into how graduating students prepare their theses are expected to run for about a month.
Inspectors are expected to focus on whether students personally chose their thesis topics and took part themselves in gathering research materials and drafting their papers, the source said. For students who have already finished their theses, examiners plan to check whether they understand the material well enough to explain it in their own words.
It remains unclear whether the ministry will lead the inspections directly, hand the task to the Pyongyang city department of education, or have universities cross-check each other’s students, according to the source.
Theses often treated as mere formality
Ghostwriting graduation theses is reportedly common at North Korean universities. Unlike science and engineering-focused schools such as Kim Chaek University of Technology or Pyongyang Medical University, some humanities departments treat a passing thesis as good enough, even without meaningful research, the source said.
“At some liberal arts universities, there’s a strong belief that all that matters is getting the thesis approved, even without any notable research achievement,” the source said. “The thesis is treated as just a formality to earn a diploma, and it’s rare to hear of anyone failing to graduate because of their thesis.”
As a result, some students have prepared for graduation by asking classmates or underclassmen skilled at writing to complete their entire thesis for them, the source said.
With news of the crackdown spreading, universities are anxious about being caught up in the fallout. Ahead of the formal inspections, schools have reportedly begun reviewing graduating students’ thesis preparation on their own. Some are requiring students to document how they gathered materials and drafted their papers, while in certain departments, faculty advisers are holding one-on-one interviews with students to directly confirm their thesis topics and content.
“Students who already received help from someone else, or whose thesis preparation is lacking, are on edge, worried that problems could surface during the university’s internal review,” the source said. “Ghostwriting is not only a problem for students, since the faculty members who supervised the thesis cannot escape responsibility either, so professors are just as on edge.”

deduped_items.body_text:
Australia news live: Man arrested after allegedly attacking woman and boy in Melbourne CBD; Richmond denies players ‘making light’ of Swans scandal in footage
Man arrested after allegedly stabbing woman with scissors and assaulting 10-year-old boy in Melbourne CBD
A man has been arrested after a boy and a woman were allegedly attacked in Melbourne’s CBD.
Victoria police said officers responded to reports of the attack at about 1pm after a 10-year-old boy from the Bass Coast region was allegedly punched in the upper body.
It is alleged that a 30-year-old woman from Cowes intervened and was allegedly stabbed in the upper body with a pair of scissors.
A 27-year-old man from Sunshine West was arrested at the scene, and police seized a pair of scissors. He remains in custody.
Authorities believe the alleged attacker and alleged victims were not known to one another.
Embattled home builder Bathla Group has been placed into voluntary administration, leaving customers in limbo in what it says is a “perfect storm” of circumstances, AAP reports.
Heavy rain across South Australia has broken various records for the month of August, with minor flood warnings issued for the Onkaparinga and Bremer rivers.
Dean Narramore, a senior meterologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, said the weather system causing the downpour is expected to shift toward the east coast tomorrow and dissipate in the evening. When it arrives, heavier falls are predicted to take place west of the ranges in New South Wales and through the Darling Downs of Queensland. Narramore said:
It’s kind of that pattern where there’s lots of rain on and west of the ranges of New South Wales, but for the east coast, maybe only 1 to 5 millimetres around Sydney.
The BoM confirmed that several locations across South Australia broke the record for daily rainfall totals in August.
Richmond players ‘embarrassed’ over Mad Monday behaviour caught on video
Mike Hytner
Richmond Football Club has insisted a group of players filmed during the club’s Mad Monday celebrations were not mocking the recent Sydney Swans scandal, while the country pub that hosted the end-of-season gathering has attempted to play down the incident.
Video footage showed one player feigning shock as he was spanked on his backside by a teammate, while another appeared to whip a fellow player with a belt. A club statement read:
Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering. The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour. The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters.
The Garfield Hotel, located 80km east of Melbourne, issued a statement earlier on Tuesday, saying the incident had been “blown out of all proportion” and that it “could not speak more highly” of the players’ behaviour. The statement read:
For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with.
They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that.
They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on.

deduped_items.title: Editorial: EU-Canadá: ¿fin del T-MEC?
deduped_items.summary: Tras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su p
deduped_items.body_text:
ras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su país “igualará los nuevos aranceles de Washington dólar por dólar, con el fin de proteger a los trabajadores, agricultores, familias y empresas canadienses”. Asimismo, reveló que “a principios de esta semana creíamos que avanzábamos hacia un acuerdo mutuamente beneficioso”, pero que a última hora “el equipo estadunidense propuso nuevas condiciones económicamente inviables e injustas” e intentó restringir “nuestra capacidad de firmar nuevos acuerdos comerciales”.
Ambas partes emplean ya abiertamente la expresión “guerra comercial” y en su más reciente réplica, el gobierno de Trump amagó ayer, por boca de su secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, con provocar un “impacto devastador” en la economía canadiense y con el pronóstico de que Ottawa volverá “muy, muy pronto” a la mesa de negociaciones. El mercurial ocupante de la Casa Blanca, de su lado, no dudó en recurrir de nuevo a la ofensiva idea de que Canadá debe convertirse en el estado 51 de su país. “Quiere los beneficios de ser un estado sin serlo”, escribió en su red Truth Social.
Tanto Canadá como México han señalado la necesidad de renovar el Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá (T-MEC) “lo antes posible” a fin de dar certidumbre a empresas y trabajadores de Norteamérica, como lo acordaron en una llamada telefónica el jueves pasado. Sin embargo, Washington se ha empecinado en mantener negociaciones bilaterales separadas con sus socios del norte y del sur, y en el caso canadiense las tratativas fracasaron y derivaron en una confrontación arancelaria que, de mantenerse, significará el fin del libre comercio entre esos dos países y, por ende, del T-MEC.
Es ya proverbial la tendencia de Trump a elevar el tono de sus amenazas y su inclinación por la violencia –no sólo la verbal– cuando se encuentra acorralado, y en el momento actual ciertamente tiene motivos para estarlo: al desastre militar que él mismo provocó en el golfo Pérsico se suman el mal desempeño de la economía y, de la mano de ambos asuntos, la caída en picada de su popularidad, justo en vísperas de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre, por no mencionar los reveses políticos y judiciales que ha venido experimentando. Por otra parte, a ojos de socios, aliados y adversarios por igual, el gobierno de Estados Unidos ha dejado de ser un interlocutor confiable, propenso a poner sobre la mesa exigencias de última hora para luego dar una patada al tablero y acusar a la contraparte del fracaso del diálogo; en ese sentido, lo ocurrido en el ámbito comercial entre Ottawa y Washington no difiere en mucho de los fallidos intentos para lograr un alto el fuego definitivo y estable entre Washington y Teherán.
Lo cierto es que para México no es una buena noticia la guerra de aranceles entre Estados Unidos y Canadá, no sólo porque ello significaría la muerte del T-MEC, que tan beneficioso ha sido para los tres países que lo integran, sino porque el gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum tendría que hacer frente a una negociación en solitario con un socio voluble, tramposo y dado a practicar la extorsión y a jugar con la incertidumbre. Pero si ese es el escenario inevitable, será preciso afrontarlo con serenidad, con espíritu constructivo y, sobre todo, con cohesión y unidad nacional.

deduped_items.body_text:
ras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su país “igualará los nuevos aranceles de Washington dólar por dólar, con el fin de proteger a los trabajadores, agricultores, familias y empresas canadienses”. Asimismo, reveló que “a principios de esta semana creíamos que avanzábamos hacia un acuerdo mutuamente beneficioso”, pero que a última hora “el equipo estadunidense propuso nuevas condiciones económicamente inviables e injustas” e intentó restringir “nuestra capacidad de firmar nuevos acuerdos comerciales”.
Ambas partes emplean ya abiertamente la expresión “guerra comercial” y en su más reciente réplica, el gobierno de Trump amagó ayer, por boca de su secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, con provocar un “impacto devastador” en la economía canadiense y con el pronóstico de que Ottawa volverá “muy, muy pronto” a la mesa de negociaciones. El mercurial ocupante de la Casa Blanca, de su lado, no dudó en recurrir de nuevo a la ofensiva idea de que Canadá debe convertirse en el estado 51 de su país. “Quiere los beneficios de ser un estado sin serlo”, escribió en su red Truth Social.
Tanto Canadá como México han señalado la necesidad de renovar el Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá (T-MEC) “lo antes posible” a fin de dar certidumbre a empresas y trabajadores de Norteamérica, como lo acordaron en una llamada telefónica el jueves pasado. Sin embargo, Washington se ha empecinado en mantener negociaciones bilaterales separadas con sus socios del norte y del sur, y en el caso canadiense las tratativas fracasaron y derivaron en una confrontación arancelaria que, de mantenerse, significará el fin del libre comercio entre esos dos países y, por ende, del T-MEC.
Es ya proverbial la tendencia de Trump a elevar el tono de sus amenazas y su inclinación por la violencia –no sólo la verbal– cuando se encuentra acorralado, y en el momento actual ciertamente tiene motivos para estarlo: al desastre militar que él mismo provocó en el golfo Pérsico se suman el mal desempeño de la economía y, de la mano de ambos asuntos, la caída en picada de su popularidad, justo en vísperas de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre, por no mencionar los reveses políticos y judiciales que ha venido experimentando. Por otra parte, a ojos de socios, aliados y adversarios por igual, el gobierno de Estados Unidos ha dejado de ser un interlocutor confiable, propenso a poner sobre la mesa exigencias de última hora para luego dar una patada al tablero y acusar a la contraparte del fracaso del diálogo; en ese sentido, lo ocurrido en el ámbito comercial entre Ottawa y Washington no difiere en mucho de los fallidos intentos para lograr un alto el fuego definitivo y estable entre Washington y Teherán.
Lo cierto es que para México no es una buena noticia la guerra de aranceles entre Estados Unidos y Canadá, no sólo porque ello significaría la muerte del T-MEC, que tan beneficioso ha sido para los tres países que lo integran, sino porque el gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum tendría que hacer frente a una negociación en solitario con un socio voluble, tramposo y dado a practicar la extorsión y a jugar con la incertidumbre. Pero si ese es el escenario inevitable, será preciso afrontarlo con serenidad, con espíritu constructivo y, sobre todo, con cohesión y unidad nacional.

deduped_items.body_text:
ras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su país “igualará los nuevos aranceles de Washington dólar por dólar, con el fin de proteger a los trabajadores, agricultores, familias y empresas canadienses”. Asimismo, reveló que “a principios de esta semana creíamos que avanzábamos hacia un acuerdo mutuamente beneficioso”, pero que a última hora “el equipo estadunidense propuso nuevas condiciones económicamente inviables e injustas” e intentó restringir “nuestra capacidad de firmar nuevos acuerdos comerciales”.
Ambas partes emplean ya abiertamente la expresión “guerra comercial” y en su más reciente réplica, el gobierno de Trump amagó ayer, por boca de su secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, con provocar un “impacto devastador” en la economía canadiense y con el pronóstico de que Ottawa volverá “muy, muy pronto” a la mesa de negociaciones. El mercurial ocupante de la Casa Blanca, de su lado, no dudó en recurrir de nuevo a la ofensiva idea de que Canadá debe convertirse en el estado 51 de su país. “Quiere los beneficios de ser un estado sin serlo”, escribió en su red Truth Social.
Tanto Canadá como México han señalado la necesidad de renovar el Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá (T-MEC) “lo antes posible” a fin de dar certidumbre a empresas y trabajadores de Norteamérica, como lo acordaron en una llamada telefónica el jueves pasado. Sin embargo, Washington se ha empecinado en mantener negociaciones bilaterales separadas con sus socios del norte y del sur, y en el caso canadiense las tratativas fracasaron y derivaron en una confrontación arancelaria que, de mantenerse, significará el fin del libre comercio entre esos dos países y, por ende, del T-MEC.
Es ya proverbial la tendencia de Trump a elevar el tono de sus amenazas y su inclinación por la violencia –no sólo la verbal– cuando se encuentra acorralado, y en el momento actual ciertamente tiene motivos para estarlo: al desastre militar que él mismo provocó en el golfo Pérsico se suman el mal desempeño de la economía y, de la mano de ambos asuntos, la caída en picada de su popularidad, justo en vísperas de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre, por no mencionar los reveses políticos y judiciales que ha venido experimentando. Por otra parte, a ojos de socios, aliados y adversarios por igual, el gobierno de Estados Unidos ha dejado de ser un interlocutor confiable, propenso a poner sobre la mesa exigencias de última hora para luego dar una patada al tablero y acusar a la contraparte del fracaso del diálogo; en ese sentido, lo ocurrido en el ámbito comercial entre Ottawa y Washington no difiere en mucho de los fallidos intentos para lograr un alto el fuego definitivo y estable entre Washington y Teherán.
Lo cierto es que para México no es una buena noticia la guerra de aranceles entre Estados Unidos y Canadá, no sólo porque ello significaría la muerte del T-MEC, que tan beneficioso ha sido para los tres países que lo integran, sino porque el gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum tendría que hacer frente a una negociación en solitario con un socio voluble, tramposo y dado a practicar la extorsión y a jugar con la incertidumbre. Pero si ese es el escenario inevitable, será preciso afrontarlo con serenidad, con espíritu constructivo y, sobre todo, con cohesión y unidad nacional.

deduped_items.summary: Tras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su p
deduped_items.body_text:
ras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su país “igualará los nuevos aranceles de Washington dólar por dólar, con el fin de proteger a los trabajadores, agricultores, familias y empresas canadienses”. Asimismo, reveló que “a principios de esta semana creíamos que avanzábamos hacia un acuerdo mutuamente beneficioso”, pero que a última hora “el equipo estadunidense propuso nuevas condiciones económicamente inviables e injustas” e intentó restringir “nuestra capacidad de firmar nuevos acuerdos comerciales”.
Ambas partes emplean ya abiertamente la expresión “guerra comercial” y en su más reciente réplica, el gobierno de Trump amagó ayer, por boca de su secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, con provocar un “impacto devastador” en la economía canadiense y con el pronóstico de que Ottawa volverá “muy, muy pronto” a la mesa de negociaciones. El mercurial ocupante de la Casa Blanca, de su lado, no dudó en recurrir de nuevo a la ofensiva idea de que Canadá debe convertirse en el estado 51 de su país. “Quiere los beneficios de ser un estado sin serlo”, escribió en su red Truth Social.
Tanto Canadá como México han señalado la necesidad de renovar el Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá (T-MEC) “lo antes posible” a fin de dar certidumbre a empresas y trabajadores de Norteamérica, como lo acordaron en una llamada telefónica el jueves pasado. Sin embargo, Washington se ha empecinado en mantener negociaciones bilaterales separadas con sus socios del norte y del sur, y en el caso canadiense las tratativas fracasaron y derivaron en una confrontación arancelaria que, de mantenerse, significará el fin del libre comercio entre esos dos países y, por ende, del T-MEC.
Es ya proverbial la tendencia de Trump a elevar el tono de sus amenazas y su inclinación por la violencia –no sólo la verbal– cuando se encuentra acorralado, y en el momento actual ciertamente tiene motivos para estarlo: al desastre militar que él mismo provocó en el golfo Pérsico se suman el mal desempeño de la economía y, de la mano de ambos asuntos, la caída en picada de su popularidad, justo en vísperas de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre, por no mencionar los reveses políticos y judiciales que ha venido experimentando. Por otra parte, a ojos de socios, aliados y adversarios por igual, el gobierno de Estados Unidos ha dejado de ser un interlocutor confiable, propenso a poner sobre la mesa exigencias de última hora para luego dar una patada al tablero y acusar a la contraparte del fracaso del diálogo; en ese sentido, lo ocurrido en el ámbito comercial entre Ottawa y Washington no difiere en mucho de los fallidos intentos para lograr un alto el fuego definitivo y estable entre Washington y Teherán.
Lo cierto es que para México no es una buena noticia la guerra de aranceles entre Estados Unidos y Canadá, no sólo porque ello significaría la muerte del T-MEC, que tan beneficioso ha sido para los tres países que lo integran, sino porque el gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum tendría que hacer frente a una negociación en solitario con un socio voluble, tramposo y dado a practicar la extorsión y a jugar con la incertidumbre. Pero si ese es el escenario inevitable, será preciso afrontarlo con serenidad, con espíritu constructivo y, sobre todo, con cohesión y unidad nacional.

deduped_items.summary: Tras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su p
deduped_items.body_text:
ras rubricar su derrota estratégica ante Irán con la amenaza de una “operación económica devastadora” contra ese país, el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, resucitó la hostilidad hacia Canadá al imponer aranceles generalizados de 50 por ciento a las importaciones de su vecino del norte, luego de que fracasó su empeño por obtener ventajas excesivas en el comercio bilateral. La respuesta del primer ministro Mark Carney no se hizo esperar: puso fin a las negociaciones y advirtió que su país “igualará los nuevos aranceles de Washington dólar por dólar, con el fin de proteger a los trabajadores, agricultores, familias y empresas canadienses”. Asimismo, reveló que “a principios de esta semana creíamos que avanzábamos hacia un acuerdo mutuamente beneficioso”, pero que a última hora “el equipo estadunidense propuso nuevas condiciones económicamente inviables e injustas” e intentó restringir “nuestra capacidad de firmar nuevos acuerdos comerciales”.
Ambas partes emplean ya abiertamente la expresión “guerra comercial” y en su más reciente réplica, el gobierno de Trump amagó ayer, por boca de su secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, con provocar un “impacto devastador” en la economía canadiense y con el pronóstico de que Ottawa volverá “muy, muy pronto” a la mesa de negociaciones. El mercurial ocupante de la Casa Blanca, de su lado, no dudó en recurrir de nuevo a la ofensiva idea de que Canadá debe convertirse en el estado 51 de su país. “Quiere los beneficios de ser un estado sin serlo”, escribió en su red Truth Social.
Tanto Canadá como México han señalado la necesidad de renovar el Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá (T-MEC) “lo antes posible” a fin de dar certidumbre a empresas y trabajadores de Norteamérica, como lo acordaron en una llamada telefónica el jueves pasado. Sin embargo, Washington se ha empecinado en mantener negociaciones bilaterales separadas con sus socios del norte y del sur, y en el caso canadiense las tratativas fracasaron y derivaron en una confrontación arancelaria que, de mantenerse, significará el fin del libre comercio entre esos dos países y, por ende, del T-MEC.
Es ya proverbial la tendencia de Trump a elevar el tono de sus amenazas y su inclinación por la violencia –no sólo la verbal– cuando se encuentra acorralado, y en el momento actual ciertamente tiene motivos para estarlo: al desastre militar que él mismo provocó en el golfo Pérsico se suman el mal desempeño de la economía y, de la mano de ambos asuntos, la caída en picada de su popularidad, justo en vísperas de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre, por no mencionar los reveses políticos y judiciales que ha venido experimentando. Por otra parte, a ojos de socios, aliados y adversarios por igual, el gobierno de Estados Unidos ha dejado de ser un interlocutor confiable, propenso a poner sobre la mesa exigencias de última hora para luego dar una patada al tablero y acusar a la contraparte del fracaso del diálogo; en ese sentido, lo ocurrido en el ámbito comercial entre Ottawa y Washington no difiere en mucho de los fallidos intentos para lograr un alto el fuego definitivo y estable entre Washington y Teherán.
Lo cierto es que para México no es una buena noticia la guerra de aranceles entre Estados Unidos y Canadá, no sólo porque ello significaría la muerte del T-MEC, que tan beneficioso ha sido para los tres países que lo integran, sino porque el gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum tendría que hacer frente a una negociación en solitario con un socio voluble, tramposo y dado a practicar la extorsión y a jugar con la incertidumbre. Pero si ese es el escenario inevitable, será preciso afrontarlo con serenidad, con espíritu constructivo y, sobre todo, con cohesión y unidad nacional.

deduped_items.title: Salen los primeros tres finalistas de México Canta
deduped_items.summary: Los Ángeles., Los cantantes Rosalba Valdez, Tiffany Galaviz y Joshua Soto son los primeros tres finalistas del certamen México Canta 2026, proyecto organizado por el gobierno de México para impulsar a las juventudes a una cultura musical sin violencia. La ceremonia, realizada ayer por la tarde en el Orpheum Theatre, en el centro de Los Ángeles, California, Estados Unidos, contó con la presencia de la secretaria de Cultura federal, Claudia Curiel de Icaza, los integrantes de la agrupación Los Tig

deduped_items.title: Trump deporta a Honduras a esposa de sargento del Ejército en servicio activo
deduped_items.summary: La esposa de un militar estadounidense fue deportada a Honduras, afectando la vida familiar y profesional del soldado. La situación refleja un patrón de deportaciones de familiares de militares bajo políticas migratorias estrictas.El sargento enfrenta desafíos para balancear sus deberes militares y el cuidado de su hija. La deportación se dio tras fallos en el proceso legal, generando críticas y una investigación legislativa.

deduped_items.title: Cartas de lectores: Pensión de privilegio, un ejemplo a seguir, hambre y pobreza

deduped_items.summary: Dispute between Washington and Beijing for global technological influence is alive in Argentina. Huawei lies at the centre of the controversy due to its participation in CALF projects in Neuquén, while the United States demands “networks of confidence” to protect data linked to Vaca Muerta. The Hidrovía waterway and the future AI projects in Bariloche complete a map where US investments co-exist with technology of Chinese origin. Leer más

deduped_items.title: The Quakes Also Exposed Venezuela’s Immunization Void
deduped_items.summary: Venezuela performed poorly before the tragedy. Then, the State refused to provide data needed to vaccinate children against preventable diseases
deduped_items.body_text:
The Quakes Also Exposed Venezuela's Immunization Void
Venezuela performed poorly before the tragedy. Then, the State refused to provide data needed to vaccinate children against preventable diseases
Runrun.es originally published this piece in Spanish. Photo by Jorge Ábrego (EFE)
“Venezuela entered this disaster burdened by a heavy immunization debt. While earthquakes do not generate epidemic outbreaks on their own, they significantly increase the risk of spreading vaccine-preventable diseases,” explained Dr. José Levy, president of the Immunization Commission at the Venezuelan Society of Childcare and Pediatrics (SVPP).
The latest report on National Immunization Coverage Estimates (WUENIC) by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) shows that in 2025, coverage for 14 vaccines the government is responsible for providing did not exceed 60%. Notably among these are pneumococcal and rotavirus vaccines, which have not been administered in the country since 2016.
For the seventh consecutive year, the Venezuelan government failed to reach 95% coverage for any vaccine under the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI)—the minimum target recommended by the WHO to protect populations against vaccine-preventable illnesses such as pertussis (whooping cough), measles, and polio, and to reduce the risk of epidemiological outbreaks.
WUENIC data revealed that vaccination coverage in Venezuela during 2025 dropped even lower than levels recorded in 2020 and 2021, when the WHO warned of global declines in immunization rates due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The WHO data reflects a 91.16% drop in public funding dedicated to mitigating the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases.
According to the Latin American Society of Vaccinology (SLV), vaccine-preventable diseases spread far more rapidly in the aftermath of socio-environmental disasters like earthquakes. In a statement released on July 7, the SLV called on the Venezuelan government to publish an inventory of vaccines available in the country to address the humanitarian emergency. To date, no government official has provided an update.
A chain of vulnerabilities
According to the SVPP, the shortage of vaccines had reached a critical tipping point a month before the earthquakes hit. On May 29, the Ministry of Health issued administrative circular No. VRSC/DGE/DI 020/2026, instructing regional epidemiology and state immunization directors to ration vaccine doses—specifically those protecting against tuberculosis (BCG); measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR); and diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTP).
The government instructed medical authorities to administer vaccines every other day, based on the number of births at each health facility, or to restrict doses exclusively to infants in their first year of life. This directive ignored the booster shots required to complete the full immunization schedules recommended by the scientific community.
“One of the primary reasons we are facing some of the worst coverage rates in Venezuela’s recent history is that our investment, or spending, on vaccines is at its lowest level in 15 years,” explained Alejandro Crespo, a pediatrician and SVPP member in Aragua state.
By 2025, less than 50% of Venezuelan children had received the complete multi-dose regimen for the DTP vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis).
According to WHO data, Venezuela once invested slightly over $48 million to meet its immunization targets. By 2025, WUENIC figures showed the government invested just over $4 million. The WHO data reflects a 91.16% drop in public funding dedicated to mitigating the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases.
“And that money does not cover operational expenses like sharps disposal containers, the red safety boxes used to discard used vials and needles. Nor does it cover healthcare staff salaries, syringes, transportation, or the cold-chain infrastructure needed to vaccinate remote areas. That figure represents spending on t

deduped_items.title: East Africa: Refinery Rivalry - Billion-Dollar Oil Projects Expose East Africa's Long-Running Regional Tensions
deduped_items.summary: [The Conversation Africa] East Africa, a region that has been working to deepen economic integration for more than 25 years, has a history of disagreements about the location of energy infrastructure. Uganda discovered oil in 2006 with the potential to pump an estimated 210,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil per day at peak production. Back in 2014, Kenya and Uganda agreed on a joint crude oil pipeline from Uganda's oil fields at Lake Albert to the Indian Ocean. But the plan was shelved in 2016. Even

deduped_items.title: D’Tigress step up World Cup preparations as Rena Wakama set to rejoin squad in Spain
deduped_items.summary: Wakama has remained in the United States because of her professional commitments with WNBA franchise Chicago Sky, but the Nigerian coach is expected to link up with her players before the World Cup gets underway The post D’Tigress step up World Cup preparations as Rena Wakama set to rejoin squad in Spain appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
deduped_items.body_text:
Nigeria’s D’Tigress are entering the final stretch of their preparations for the 2026 FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup, with head coach Rena Wakama expected to rejoin the team ahead of the tournament in Germany.
Wakama has remained in the United States because of her professional commitments with WNBA franchise Chicago Sky, but the Nigerian coach is expected to link up with her players before the World Cup gets underway.
The tournament is scheduled to run from 4-13 September, with D’Tigress set to move to Zaragoza, Spain, for the final phase of their preparations.
Wakama has continued to combine her responsibilities as Nigeria’s head coach with her role as an assistant coach at the Chicago Sky. The WNBA franchise confirmed her appointment to its coaching staff in April under head coach Tyler Marsh.
Nigeria began their World Cup preparations with a training camp in Chicago from 29 July to 2 August before travelling to China for a three-game exhibition series.
D’Tigress then moved to Spain, where they faced some of Europe’s leading basketball nations as part of their continued preparations.
The final phase of the camp in Zaragoza will feature further preparation games against Mali and Puerto Rico before Nigeria travel to Berlin for the World Cup.
D’Tigress face concerns after difficult warm-up run
The African champions have endured a challenging build-up to the tournament, winning just one of their five warm-up games so far.
Nigeria began their exhibition series in China with consecutive defeats, losing 70-67 and 69-65 before bouncing back to record an encouraging 88-77 victory on 12 August.
However, their latest outings in Tenerife exposed further concerns, with D’Tigress suffering heavy defeats against two of Europe’s strongest teams.
They were beaten 83-58 by Spain on 21 August before Belgium handed them another emphatic defeat, winning 90-55 the following day.
The results have highlighted areas that will need to be addressed during the final phase of preparations as Nigeria target another strong showing on the global stage.
Despite the difficult warm-up campaign, D’Tigress head into Germany as the reigning African champions after securing their fifth consecutive FIBA Women’s AfroBasket title with a hard-fought 78-64 victory over Mali in the 2025 final.
Their continental dominance followed an historic campaign at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where Nigeria became the first African team to reach the quarter-finals of the Olympic basketball tournament.
Nigeria secured an automatic place at the 2026 World Cup after winning the 2025 FIBA Women’s AfroBasket, although they still participated in the qualifying tournament in Lyon-Villeurbanne, France, where they endured a difficult campaign, winning two and losing three of their five games.
Nigeria chasing another World Cup quarter-final
The tournament in Germany will mark D’Tigress’ third appearance at the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup, following previous appearances in 2006 and 2018.
READ ALSO: D’Tigress turn focus to Spain after China tour victory
Their best performance came at the 2018 edition, where they reached the quarter-finals before finishing eighth overall.
Nigeria repeated that feat four years later at the 2022 World Cup, reaching the last eight in a campaign that further established D’Tigress as one of Africa’s leading basketball teams.
With less than two weeks before the 2026 tournament tips off, Wakama’s return will be an important part of Nigeria’s final preparations as the reigning African champions look to turn a difficult pre-tournament run into another memorable World Cup campaign.

deduped_items.summary: Les Émirats arabes unis sont devenus, en quelques années, un acteur économique et stratégique majeur en Afrique. deduped_items.title: RDC: dans l’ombre d’Ebola, la flambée des cas de choléra inquiète l'OMS
deduped_items.summary: Alors que l’épidémie d’Ebola concentre l’attention en République démocratique du Congo, le pays reste confronté à une flambée prolongée de choléra. Près de 39 500 cas suspects et 1 173 décès ont été enregistrés depuis le début de l'année 2026. La létalité est surtout beaucoup plus élevée dans les provinces qui ne sont pas habituellement touchées. L’OMS et Médecins sans frontières (MSF) alertent sur les faiblesses de la prise en charge et le risque de voir les autres urgences sanitaires reléguées

Le ministère de l'Éducation instaure un système à trois niveaux – vert, orange et rouge – selon l'intensité de la transmission. deduped_items.title: “The Strategy of Terrorism”
deduped_items.summary: A quarter century before 9/11, an upsurge in global terrorism prompted the historian David Fromkin to examine its purpose and method. Terrorism was a strategy of the weak, Fromkin wrote in these pages, but modern technology had enabled it “to enter the political arena on a new scale.” And its surprising success seemed to be due, in large part, “to a miscomprehension of the strategy by its opponents.”

deduped_items.title: Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
deduped_items.summary: The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.
deduped_items.body_text:
Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.”
A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic. Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds. There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses.
Questioning colleges is normal. There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost, and is that more than families can pay? Who gets in, and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium.
On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education, to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself.
I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Jack Stripling: We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.
Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and around the country millions of students are getting ready to head back to school, if they’re not already in class. So today, we need to think about education in uncertain times.
Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school. In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed. My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t. In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges.
But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve. Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions. Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project. The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures.
How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year?
Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague. And he joins me now to discuss.
 
 Let’s get to questions.
Jack, welcome to the show.
Stripling: Adam Harris, so g

deduped_items.body_text:
Listen on
Nach der Sommerpause trifft sich die Bundesregierung zur ersten Klausur nach dem Kabinettsumbau im brandenburgischen Schloss Neuhardenberg. Der Kanzler fordert Disziplin, aber die Konflikte belasten die Koalition weiterhin merklich. Rasmus Buchsteiner liefert dazu die ersten Einschätzungen direkt aus Neuhardenberg.
Im 200-Sekunden-Interview stellt sich der SPD-Fraktionschef Matthias Miersch den Fragen zum politischen Herbst. Er zeigt sich überzeugt, dass Friedrich Merz trotz aktuell schlechter Umfragen bis zum Ende der Amtszeit Kanzler bleibt. Außerdem ordnet er die Rentenpläne und die Umfragewerte der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt ein.
Nachdem ein pauschales Social-Media-Verbot für Jugendliche in Frankreich gescheitert ist, sortiert Larissa Kögl von POLITICO PRO „Technologie & KI am Morgen“ die teils unübersichtliche Debatte in Deutschland und der EU. Dabei zeigen sich auch deutliche Differenzen zwischen der zuständigen Ministerin Karin Prien und weiten Teilen der Union. Nun wird auf klare Richtlinien aus Brüssel und erste Zeichen von Ursula von der Leyen gehofft.
Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

deduped_items.body_text:
Listen on
Nach der Sommerpause trifft sich die Bundesregierung zur ersten Klausur nach dem Kabinettsumbau im brandenburgischen Schloss Neuhardenberg. Der Kanzler fordert Disziplin, aber die Konflikte belasten die Koalition weiterhin merklich. Rasmus Buchsteiner liefert dazu die ersten Einschätzungen direkt aus Neuhardenberg.
Im 200-Sekunden-Interview stellt sich der SPD-Fraktionschef Matthias Miersch den Fragen zum politischen Herbst. Er zeigt sich überzeugt, dass Friedrich Merz trotz aktuell schlechter Umfragen bis zum Ende der Amtszeit Kanzler bleibt. Außerdem ordnet er die Rentenpläne und die Umfragewerte der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt ein.
Nachdem ein pauschales Social-Media-Verbot für Jugendliche in Frankreich gescheitert ist, sortiert Larissa Kögl von POLITICO PRO „Technologie & KI am Morgen“ die teils unübersichtliche Debatte in Deutschland und der EU. Dabei zeigen sich auch deutliche Differenzen zwischen der zuständigen Ministerin Karin Prien und weiten Teilen der Union. Nun wird auf klare Richtlinien aus Brüssel und erste Zeichen von Ursula von der Leyen gehofft.
Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

deduped_items.title: Jason Arday and the new politics of plagiarism
deduped_items.summary: The resignation and death of the Cambridge professor is the latest chapter in a centuries-old struggle over originality and intellectual ownership – one intensified by the rise of generative AI.
deduped_items.body_text:
After a meteoric rise to the top ranks of British academia, scholar Jason Arday was found dead at his London home on Aug. 14, 2026.
Arday had spent weeks fighting plagiarism accusations. The way they took on a life of their own in the media ecosystem is a stark reminder of the steep price people can pay in a culture that has made originality a kind of moral virtue.
In 2023, at age 38, he had been appointed to a professorship in sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the youngest Black professor in the institution’s 800-year history.
Nine days before his death, Arday had resigned from his faculty position. He was facing growing criticism about improbable and inconsistent details appearing in his memoir, scheduled to be released in the coming weeks by Simon & Schuster. Arday’s publisher had stood by him, lauding the academic’s “professionalism and integrity.”
But the originality of Arday’s dissertation and his other academic work was also coming under scrutiny, leading to multiple allegations of plagiarism.
Arday vehemently denied the accusations, suggesting that any mistakes were the result of his autism. He also claimed that his accusers were motivated by racism.
The controversy over Arday’s work reflects an ongoing trend of ideological opponents levying plagiarism accusations to undermine one another. I think it’s also worth exploring why such attacks continue to be so enticing – and so effective.
Shifting standards for originality
Plagiarism can be defined as the appropriation of someone else’s words or ideas without acknowledgment or compensation.
In the ancient world, plagiarism was viewed quite negatively: The word “plagiarism” actually means “kidnapper” in Latin, and the Roman poet Horace described literary theft like a crow making itself beautiful with stolen feathers.
But in my 2026 book, “Strikingly Similar,” I explore how, throughout the medieval period, the Renaissance and into the early modern era, an ethos of “imitatio” prevailed. Chaucer, Shakespeare and Milton are examples of authors who hewed closely to writers who had come before them. These writers freely borrowed plots, characters and rhetorical devices in the service of their own work.
True originality came to be viewed in a positive light only gradually, and it eventually developed into the modern concept of intellectual property, in which the creative products of human ingenuity are viewed as tangible assets. Treating creative works as property, in turn, created the legal framework to protect them.
The German artist Albrecht Dürer initiated one of the first known intellectual property lawsuits. In 1506, he asked the Venetian government to stop the Italian engraver Marcantonio Raimondi from copying his woodcuts. Dürer was only partly successful: It was decided that Raimondi could continue copying Dürer’s work, but he was prohibited from also copying the artist’s distinctive monogram.
In the 19th century, as the result of lobbying by authors such as Charles Dickens, the British Parliament enacted the Copyright Act of 1842. This statute greatly expanded the protections granted to authors. It would take another 50 years, however, before foreign authors like Dickens enjoyed similar protections under U.S. copyright law.
Today, the situation that existed during the Renaissance has almost totally reversed itself.
In Europe, groups of scholars have banded together to investigate allegations of plagiarism. Using crowdsourcing techniques, VroniPlag Wiki in Germany and Dissernet in Russia have exposed numerous instances of plagiarism by public servants in their dissertations and academic publications.
The work of VroniPlag Wiki alone has led to several German universities revoking doctoral degrees they had awarded to elected and appointed government officials.
Plagiarism becomes political
Today, accusations of plagiarism have become a potent way to undermine someone’s credibility. If a claim is substantiated, the plagiarist is seen as sloppy

These writers freely borrowed plots, characters and rhetorical devices in the service of their own work.
True originality came to be viewed in a positive light only gradually, and it eventually developed into the modern concept of intellectual property, in which the creative products of human ingenuity are viewed as tangible assets. Treating creative works as property, in turn, created the legal framework to protect them.
The German artist Albrecht Dürer initiated one of the first known intellectual property lawsuits. In 1506, he asked the Venetian government to stop the Italian engraver Marcantonio Raimondi from copying his woodcuts. Dürer was only partly successful: It was decided that Raimondi could continue copying Dürer’s work, but he was prohibited from also copying the artist’s distinctive monogram.
In the 19th century, as the result of lobbying by authors such as Charles Dickens, the British Parliament enacted the Copyright Act of 1842. This statute greatly expanded the protections granted to authors. It would take another 50 years, however, before foreign authors like Dickens enjoyed similar protections under U.S. copyright law.

In 2023, at age 38, he had been appointed to a professorship in sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the youngest Black professor in the institution’s 800-year history.

But the originality of Arday’s dissertation and his other academic work was also coming under scrutiny, leading to multiple allegations of plagiarism.
Arday vehemently denied the accusations, suggesting that any mistakes were the result of his autism. He also claimed that his accusers were motivated by racism.

deduped_items.title: UNESCO: Why so many of Africa’s natural treasures remain ‘in danger’
deduped_items.summary: The continent has relatively few natural sites listed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, but is overrepresented among those classified as under threat. From Garamba National Park in DRC to Djoudj National Park in Senegal, here is an infographic-based analysis of the threats facing the continent’s natural wonders.
deduped_items.body_text:
UNESCO: Why so many of Africa’s natural treasures remain ‘in danger’
The continent has relatively few natural sites listed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, but is overrepresented among those classified as under threat. From Garamba National Park in DRC to Djoudj National Park in Senegal, here is an infographic-based analysis of the threats facing the continent’s natural wonders.
By
Julie Desrousseaux
Published
on August 25, 2026
at
06:30 am (GMT +1)
On 29 July, four new African sites joined UNESCO’s prestigious World Heritage List. Among them was Boma-Badingilo, a natural jewel of South Sudan. At the same time, the organisation updated the classification of Garamba National Park in Democratic Republic of Congo, formally recognising the exceptional value of its ecosystems.
It was a mixed blessing: both Garamba and Boma-Badingilo also feature on the List of World Heritage in Danger, which includes sites threatened by armed conflict, natural disasters, poaching, urbanisation and pollution, among other risks.

It was a mixed blessing: both Garamba and Boma-Badingilo also feature on the List of World Heritage in Danger, which includes sites threatened by armed conflict, natural disasters, poaching, urbanisation and pollution, among other risks.

deduped_items.title: واشنطن تعلن "يوم النصر الاقتصادي" على إيران وطهران تعتبره "إقرارا بالهزيمة"
deduped_items.summary: صعّدت الولايات المتحدة ضغوطها على إيران بإعلان وزير الخزانة سكوت بيسنت عقوبات جديدة وتهديد شركائها التجاريين بإجراءات ثانوية، فيما تواصلت التحركات الدبلوماسية بشأن مضيق هرمز مع زيارة مرتقبة لوزير الخارجية العُماني بدر البوسعيدي إلى طهران ومباحثات لقائد الجيش الباكستاني عاصم منير. وفي البحر الأحمر، تعرضت ناقلة لهجوم قبالة السعودية، بينما رفعت واشنطن سوريا من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب، وقُتل خمسة فلسطينيين في غزة ومنعت إسرائيل نائبين أوروبيين من زيارة الضفة الغربية.

deduped_items.summary: صعّدت الولايات المتحدة ضغوطها على إيران بإعلان وزير الخزانة سكوت بيسنت عقوبات جديدة وتهديد شركائها التجاريين بإجراءات ثانوية، فيما تواصلت التحركات الدبلوماسية بشأن مضيق هرمز مع زيارة مرتقبة لوزير الخارجية العُماني بدر البوسعيدي إلى طهران ومباحثات لقائد الجيش الباكستاني عاصم منير. وفي البحر الأحمر، تعرضت ناقلة لهجوم قبالة السعودية، بينما رفعت واشنطن سوريا من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب، وقُتل خمسة فلسطينيين في غزة ومنعت إسرائيل نائبين أوروبيين من زيارة الضفة الغربية.

deduped_items.title: EE. UU. busca la "asfixia económica" de Irán con sanciones a 60 personas, empresas y embarcaciones
deduped_items.summary: La inflación de Irán se acerca al 90% interanual, frente al 60% registrado a comienzos de año, mientras Estados Unidos amplía su estrategia de “asfixia económica” contra Teherán para ahogar cualquier fuente vinculada, según Estados Unidos, con los ingresos petroleros, la adquisición de armas y operaciones cibernéticas de la República Islámica. La ofensiva también amenaza con excluir del sistema financiero basado en el dólar a quienes faciliten operaciones de lavado de dinero en nombre de la naci

deduped_items.title: Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche: Beyond sorrow
deduped_items.summary: On the sidelines of the 2026 Rimini Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche, who have come to be known as “sisters in sorrow", speak to Vatican News about the tragedy that unites them. Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all

Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche: Beyond sorrow
Below is a transcript of the interview with Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche. It has been translated from French and edited for fluency and readability.
You can watch the full interview, in French, here.
Q: Roseline, what prompted you to reach out to Nassera?
Roseline Hamel: It was a question I asked myself every day. I wondered who could possibly be suffering more than I was. It was a long journey, lasting almost a year, during which I kept asking God that question. All my conversations with Him were like a prayer, but I received no answer.
Then one morning, I turned to God and said: âMy God, tell me who could be suffering more than I am.â To me, it did not seem possible.
The following morning, I began thinking about this woman I did not know - this mother, who was a mother just like me. I reversed our roles and tried to put myself in her place. I imagined her pain, her torment and the months of struggle she had endured with her young son, who had allowed himself to be drawn down a path his mother would never have wanted for him.
I imagined the contemptuous looks she must have faced and the cloak of guilt she had to bear as a parent. That was when I realised I had found the person who might be suffering more than I was.
I said to myself: âThatâs it. I have found this path back to life, the sense of meaning I have been searching for since the funeral and since returning home.â Then I told myself: âNow, Roseline, you must do something. You must find the way to the house where this mother lives.â
Q: Nassera, what did you feel when Roseline knocked on your door for the first time?
Nassera Kermiche: It was also a long journey, because we first spoke on the telephone. At the beginning, our conversations were very brief. Then, little by little, a genuine dialogue developed between us.
One day, Roseline asked me: âIf I come to Saint-Étienne, would you be willing to meet me?â I replied: âOf course. I have been waiting for you for a long time.â
I had been hoping for that meeting for quite some time. I had already tried to meet the religious sisters who had been inside the church when the attack took place, but it had not been possible.
I was therefore very happy to be able to meet Roseline. When she arrived at my door and I opened it, I was so emotional and so happy that no words would come out of my mouth except: âForgive me, forgive me.â That was all I could say, because I needed her forgiveness.
Q: Roseline, you speak of forgiveness as a journey. Was there a particular moment when you understood or felt that forgiveness was possible?
Roseline Hamel: I had never really thought about the difficulty of forgiveness. Perhaps I had never had reason to. Forgiving is, of course, always difficult, and it depends on the magnitude of the offence.
Until then, I had faced the ordinary difficulties of life. As my daughter would say to me: âLet it go, Mum.â And I would let things go quite easily because I had other things to live for. When you are raising children, you cannot dwell indefinitely on something that has hurt or offended you.
But in the situation that brings us together today, offering forgiveness appeared, in the eyes of society, to be an immense and almost impossible undertaking. Why? Because we do not share the same religion and everything appeared destined to divide us.
That tragic day, that day of deadly violence which we both experienced, should have sown hatred towards this family. But hatred leads to revenge, violence and the destruction of our own humanity.
I do not know whether it was the sacrifice of those lives that meant we received the grace of God not to feel hatred. No member of my family felt it.
Three days before the funeral, the Archbishop of Rouen came to my sisterâs home to help us organise it. There were twelve of us in a small flat intended for four people. Before we began, he asked us a question: âDo you feel hatred?â
I wondered why he was asking us that, bec

Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all

Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all
deduped_items.body_text:
Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche: Beyond sorrow
Below is a transcript of the interview with Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche. It has been translated from French and edited for fluency and readability.
You can watch the full interview, in French, here.
Q: Roseline, what prompted you to reach out to Nassera?
Roseline Hamel: It was a question I asked myself every day. I wondered who could possibly be suffering more than I was. It was a long journey, lasting almost a year, during which I kept asking God that question. All my conversations with Him were like a prayer, but I received no answer.
Then one morning, I turned to God and said: âMy God, tell me who could be suffering more than I am.â To me, it did not seem possible.
The following morning, I began thinking about this woman I did not know - this mother, who was a mother just like me. I reversed our roles and tried to put myself in her place. I imagined her pain, her torment and the months of struggle she had endured with her young son, who had allowed himself to be drawn down a path his mother would never have wanted for him.
I imagined the contemptuous looks she must have faced and the cloak of guilt she had to bear as a parent. That was when I realised I had found the person who might be suffering more than I was.
I said to myself: âThatâs it. I have found this path back to life, the sense of meaning I have been searching for since the funeral and since returning home.â Then I told myself: âNow, Roseline, you must do something. You must find the way to the house where this mother lives.â
Q: Nassera, what did you feel when Roseline knocked on your door for the first time?
Nassera Kermiche: It was also a long journey, because we first spoke on the telephone. At the beginning, our conversations were very brief. Then, little by little, a genuine dialogue developed between us.
One day, Roseline asked me: âIf I come to Saint-Étienne, would you be willing to meet me?â I replied: âOf course. I have been waiting for you for a long time.â
I had been hoping for that meeting for quite some time. I had already tried to meet the religious sisters who had been inside the church when the attack took place, but it had not been possible.
I was therefore very happy to be able to meet Roseline. When she arrived at my door and I opened it, I was so emotional and so happy that no words would come out of my mouth except: âForgive me, forgive me.â That was all I could say, because I needed her forgiveness.
Q: Roseline, you speak of forgiveness as a journey. Was there a particular moment when you understood or felt that forgiveness was possible?
Roseline Hamel: I had never really thought about the difficulty of forgiveness. Perhaps I had never had reason to. Forgiving is, of course, always difficult, and it depends on the magnitude of the offence.
Until then, I had faced the ordinary difficulties of life. As my daughter would say to me: âLet it go, Mum.â And I would let things go quite easily because I had other things to live for. When you are raising children, you cannot dwell indefinitely on something that has hurt or offended you.
But in the situation that brings us together today, offering forgiveness appeared, in the eyes of society, to be an immense and almost impossible undertaking. Why? Because we do not share the same religion and everything appeared destined to divide us.
That tragic day, that day of deadly violence which we both experienced, should have sown hatred towards this family. But hatred leads to revenge, violence and the destruction of our own humanity.
I do not know whether it was the sacrifice of those lives that meant we received the grace of God not to feel hatred. No member of my family felt it.
Three days before the funeral, the Archbishop of Rouen came to my sisterâs home to help us organise it. There were twelve of us in a small flat intended for four people. Before we began, he asked us a question: âDo you feel hatred?â
I wondered why he was asking us that, bec
